strengths: Highly practical and realistic formulation: The paper proposes training weakly-supervised video anomaly detection (WVAD) models without collecting any real abnormal videos, relying instead on pseudo-anomalies generated from a small pool of normal images and abnormal class names.

Well-designed Class-Aware Pseudo-Anomaly Generator (CA-PAG): Using CLIP-based initial image selection ensures that the seed frames for video generation are contextually relevant to the class (e.g., street scenes for road accidents), and VLM-based prompt refinement significantly improves generation consistency and motion plausibility.

Effective Domain-Aligned Regularized Module (DARM): To mitigate the covariate shift and feature magnitude inflation common in generated videos, DARM effectively incorporates an adversarial domain-alignment objective and a usage-aware memory bank update. This prevents the MIL model from overfitting to high-magnitude synthetic features.

Strong quantitative and qualitative results: PA-VAD achieves 98.2% on ShanghaiTech (outperforming methods trained on real anomalies) and 82.5% on UCF-Crime (outperforming the unsupervised state-of-the-art by 1.9%). Detailed ablations validate each component of the proposed framework.
weaknesses: High generation cost: As mentioned in the supplementary material, generating a single pseudo-abnormal clip takes around 9 minutes on a high-end RTX 6000 Ada GPU, resulting in ~30 hours of generation time for ShanghaiTech and ~55 hours for UCF-Crime. This is a non-trivial computational overhead before training can begin.

Gap in complex, long-horizon scenarios: While performing exceptionally on ShanghaiTech, the method still struggles on UCF-Crime compared to real-supervised WVAD models (82.5% vs 87.0% for UR-DMU) due to the limitation of current I2V diffusion models in generating complex, context-heavy, or long-term anomalous events (e.g., shoplifting or subtle abuse).

Dependence on pre-trained large models: The success of the pipeline is heavily reliant on multiple large-scale foundation models, specifically Wan2.2 (14B parameter video generator), Qwen3 (30B VLM), and CLIP, which may limit execution in resource-constrained environments.

strengths: Highly Practical and Realistic Problem Setting: Training a weakly-supervised video anomaly detection (WVAD) model without relying on scarce and expensive real abnormal videos is a highly valuable goal. Leveraging generative models to create pseudo-anomalies provides a scalable alternative.

Well-Designed Generation & Training Pipeline: The proposed framework is technically sound. Using CLIP to anchor seed images prevents domain shift in backgrounds (e.g., matching a street scene for road accidents), while VLM-driven prompt refinement improves motion and temporal coherence.

Addressing Feature Norm Discrepancy: The paper correctly identifies and addresses a critical issue: generated videos often exhibit inflated feature norms that bias Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) training. The introduction of the Domain-Aligned Regularized Module (DARM) successfully regularizes the training and mitigates this bias.

Impressive Empirical Results: The model achieves 98.2% on ShanghaiTech and 82.5% on UCF-Crime. On ShanghaiTech, it even outperforms fully-supervised WVAD models trained on real abnormal videos, which is a remarkable result.
weaknesses: High Computational and Resource Requirements: Generating video clips via large diffusion models is extremely time-consuming and resource-intensive. According to the supplementary material, generating a single video takes nearly 10 minutes on an NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada GPU, and generating the entire training set takes 30 to 55 hours. This limits the quick deployment and scalability of the method.

Reliance on Prior Class Metadata: The generator requires explicit abnormal class names (e.g., 'Explosion', 'Assault') to synthesize the pseudo-anomalies. This makes the comparison to some UVAD (unsupervised) methods slightly unfair, as standard UVAD methods do not assume prior knowledge of what specific anomaly categories will appear during inference.

Limitations with Complex/Fine-Grained Anomalies: As shown in Figure 10(e) (Shoplifting), the diffusion generator struggles with long-horizon, highly context-dependent, or fine-grained anomalies. This explains the performance gap compared to fully-supervised WVAD on UCF-Crime (82.5% vs 87.0%), where such complex events are common.

Incremental Architectural Novelty: While the overall system is clever and highly effective, the core components—image-to-video diffusion (Wan2.2), CLIP retrieval, VLM-based prompting, and GRL-based domain adaptation—are largely standard tools. The underlying VAD classifier is built directly on top of the existing UR-DMU backbone.

strengths: The paper introduces a practical and highly relevant setting: training a weakly-supervised video anomaly detection (VAD) model without using any real abnormal videos, relying instead on high-quality synthesized pseudo-anomalies.

The Class-Aware Pseudo-Anomaly Generator (CA-PAG) is well-designed, leveraging CLIP-guided retrieval to anchor the initial images in the target domain and a VLM (Qwen3) to refine coarse labels into realistic, temporally consistent prompts.

The paper identifies an important and often overlooked issue of generated video data: feature norm inflation. The proposed Domain-Aligned Regularized Module (DARM) addresses this feature norm discrepancy and MIL bias effectively through domain adversarial training and a usage-aware memory update rule.

The proposed method achieves impressive results, outperforming all unsupervised VAD baselines on both ShanghaiTech and UCF-Crime, and even outperforming several state-of-the-art weakly-supervised VAD methods that rely on real abnormal videos.

The manuscript is exceptionally well-written, with clear figures, comprehensive ablation studies, and detailed supplementary material that details generation costs, failure cases, and hyperparameters.
weaknesses: The generation overhead is quite high. Synthesizing 140 video clips for ShanghaiTech and 260 for UCF-Crime takes approximately 30 and 55 hours respectively on an NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada GPU. This makes the data preparation phase computationally expensive.

The method heavily depends on massive, high-performing foundational models (CLIP, Qwen3-30B-A3B, and Wan2.2-14B). There is no analysis of how sensitive the VAD performance is to the choice or scale of these models (e.g., using smaller VLMs or older generation models).

The setup assumes prior knowledge of the specific anomaly class names (e.g., 'Burglary', 'Explosion') to run retrieval and prompt generation. While this fits the WVAD paradigm, it is more restrictive than classical UVAD, which does not require knowing which abnormal classes might occur in advance.

As noted in the limitations, the framework struggles to synthesize context-heavy, long-horizon anomalies (like subtle shoplifting or long-term abuse), which explains why the performance on UCF-Crime still lags significantly behind the best fully supervised WVAD methods.

strengths: Strong motivation and practical relevance: Eliminating the dependency on collecting real abnormal videos is highly valuable due to privacy, safety constraints, and the rarity of certain anomaly classes.

Excellent empirical insight: The paper identifies a key issue when training detectors purely on diffusion-synthesized videos—specifically, the spatiotemporal magnitude bias (abnormally large feature norms) which leads to a feature magnitude shortcut in Multiple Instance Learning (MIL).
Effective technical design: The proposed Domain-Aligned Regularized Module (DARM) successfully handles this magnitude bias by combining domain adversarial training with usage-aware memory updates.

Impressive empirical results: PA-VAD outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised methods and even surpasses some weakly-supervised models trained on real abnormal footage on ShanghaiTech and XD-Violence.
Thorough evaluation: The inclusion of open-set generalizations, quantitative analyses of feature norms, generation quality metrics, and clear ablation studies make the findings highly convincing.
weaknesses: Inconsistent baseline backbones: The proposed method uses Qwen2.5-VL features as the frozen clip-level backbone, while older weakly-supervised methods (like CMRL or UR-DMU) are evaluated on older backbones like I3D or C3D. A comparative evaluation using identical feature extractors for all methods would isolate the performance gains of the training framework from the strength of the backbone.

High computational cost for pseudo-data generation: Generating the offline pseudo-anomalies requires substantial GPU hours (e.g., 55 hours on dual RTX 6000 GPUs for UCF-Crime), which limits the training pipeline's immediate scalability for larger or customized target sets.

Performance limitations on complex anomalies: As noted in the limitations, the method still struggles with long-horizon, context-heavy anomalies (e.g., shoplifting or subtle abuse) where the video generator fails to create temporally coherent abnormal cues.

strengths: Practical and Novel Framework: Training a weakly-supervised video anomaly detection (VAD) model without collecting real abnormal training videos is highly desirable due to privacy, scarcity, and safety constraints. PA-VAD presents a successful pipeline that pairs real normal videos with generated pseudo-abnormal videos.

Insightful Discovery of Magnitude Bias: The paper identifies an important and overlooked issue in using synthesized pseudo anomalies: they suffer from a severe spatiotemporal magnitude bias (inflated feature norms) that acts as an optimization shortcut during Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) training.

Well-designed Mitigation Module (DARM): The proposed Domain-Aligned Regularized Module elegantly addresses the magnitude bias using domain-adversarial alignment and a usage-aware memory update. Table 5b convincingly shows how DARM restores the pseudo-anomaly feature norms back to the range of real anomalies.

Strong Empirical Results: The method achieves state-of-the-art results on ShanghaiTech (98.2% AUC) and XD-Violence (95.1% AUC) under the pseudo-only setting, even outperforming several methods trained on real abnormal videos.

Rigorous Ablation Studies: The ablation analyses (Table 5a, 5b, Table 6) are thorough and clearly isolate the impact of initial image selection, VLM prompt refinement, domain alignment, and the usage-aware update.
weaknesses: High Computational and Generation Cost: Generating the pseudo-anomaly videos is computationally intensive. As stated in the supplementary material, generating the training set for UCF-Crime takes about 55 hours on two high-end NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada GPUs. This high offline generation cost limits the immediate scalability of the framework for larger or more dynamic environments.

Heavy Dependency on External Foundation Models: The success of the pipeline is tightly coupled with the capability of modern foundation models (Wan 2.2, Qwen3/Qwen2.5-VL, and CLIP). A discussion on how errors or domain shifts in these models propagate to VAD performance would improve completeness.

Performance Gap on Complex Datasets: There is still a noticeable performance gap on UCF-Crime (82.5% AUC) compared to weakly-supervised methods trained on real abnormal videos (e.g., 87.0% for UR-DMU). Synthesizing long-horizon, context-heavy anomalies remains a major hurdle.

Sensitivity to Hyperparameters: The training relies on several loss weights and coefficients (e.g., lambda_1, lambda_2, lambda_da, lambda_dist, beta in Table 2). A sensitivity analysis of these parameters would help verify the stability of the proposed DARM objectives.

strengths: The paper introduces a highly practical paradigm (PA-VAD) that eliminates the need for real abnormal training videos by leveraging diffusion-synthesized pseudo-anomalies.

The discovery of the 'pseudo-induced spatiotemporal magnitude bias' in synthesized video features is an insightful empirical finding, backed by quantitative evidence showing massive feature norm inflation in the detector's latent space.
The proposed Domain-Aligned Regularized Module (DARM) addresses this bias elegantly through domain-adversarial training and usage-aware memory prototype updates.

The paper achieves state-of-the-art results on several challenging VAD datasets (ShanghaiTech, UCF-Crime, XD-Violence) under the pseudo-only setting, and shows superior generalization to unseen classes in open-set scenarios.
The ablation study is comprehensive, clearly isolating the effects of initial image selection, prompt refinement, domain alignment, and usage-aware updates.
weaknesses: Confounding Feature Extractor Comparison: The proposed method uses a powerful modern vision-language backbone (Qwen2.5-VL) as the video feature extractor, whereas older baseline methods in Table 4 use I3D, C3D, or InternVL2. It remains unclear how much of the performance advantage over previous real-training baselines is due to the advanced backbone versus the pseudo-data pipeline. Including a baseline like UR-DMU trained on Real/Real with the Qwen2.5-VL backbone would clarify this.

High Generation Cost: Generating pseudo-videos relies on Wan 2.2 (14B parameter model) and Qwen-3 (30B), requiring substantial GPU memory (96GB per GPU) and wall-clock time (e.g., 55 hours for UCF-Crime on high-end Ada GPUs). This high resource requirement should be highlighted more clearly as a practical limitation.

Ambiguity in Pseudo-Normal Generation: The prompt design and generation process for the 'pseudo-normal' videos (used for domain alignment) are not fully detailed in either the main text or the supplementary material.
